messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 51
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Tax Inspector
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
- Pcl5: 39

# The Weight of Numbers

Boon-Nam is a 51-year-old Thai man who has worked for the national revenue department for nearly two decades. He is precise by nature — meticulous with figures, careful with language, someone who built his professional identity around the idea that if you follow the rules correctly, outcomes are predictable and fair. His personal life, it turns out, did not work that way.

For six years in his late thirties and early forties, Boon-Nam was in a relationship with a man he describes quietly as "very charming at the beginning." The violence began gradually — a shove during an argument, a slap that was followed by apologies and flowers — and escalated over time into something Boon-Nam still struggles to name directly. He was punched, choked on more than one occasion, and once thrown against a kitchen counter hard enough to fracture two ribs. He told his colleagues he had fallen. He told himself the same thing for a long time. He ended the relationship eleven years ago and, within two years, married his wife, a woman he describes with genuine warmth. He has not spoken to anyone in his personal life about what happened during those six years.

What Boon-Nam notices now, in his fifties, is that the past does not stay in the past. He sits across from taxpayers every day — auditing accounts, asking questions, watching people's faces when they feel cornered or caught — and certain moments ambush him without warning. When a male client raises his voice in frustration, Boon-Nam's body responds before his mind does. His chest tightens, his hands go still on the desk, and he finds himself calculating the distance to the door. He has become known among colleagues as unusually calm under pressure, and he lets them believe that. What they cannot see is that the calm is something he is holding in place with both hands.

At home, he sleeps poorly. He wakes between two and four in the morning with a physical alertness that feels like danger, though his bedroom is quiet and his wife is beside him. He rarely tells her he has woken. He lies still and waits for morning, reviewing tax codes in his head as a way of steadying himself — numbers as anchor. He has stopped sleeping on his left side because that is the side he was lying on during one of the worst nights, and his body has apparently filed that information away as a permanent warning.

He avoids certain parts of the city where he and his former partner used to go together. He has rerouted his commute twice over the years to avoid a particular street. He tells himself this is about traffic. He knows it is not.

What troubles Boon-Nam most, and what finally brought him to a psychologist's office, is a growing sense of numbness toward his wife and their two adult children. He loves them — he is certain of this — but he often feels as though he is watching his family from behind glass. He attends dinners, he asks about their days, he is present in every outward sense. But something that used to feel natural now feels performed, and he is frightened by the distance he cannot close. His wife has noticed. She has not said so directly, but he sees it in the way she watches him sometimes, and the thought that he might be failing her in some invisible way is, he says, harder to sit with than anything else.

He came to the first session in a pressed shirt, carrying a leather folder he did not open. He spoke carefully, choosing words the way he chooses which accounts to flag — only what he could be certain of. By the third session, he brought the folder again and still did not open it. But he talked about the kitchen counter. It was the first time he had said it aloud to anyone.
